title: Comparing kumquat with lime
text: d_multitwo two predictors (x, y) binary class (, B). class boundary made four pieces: horizontal edge, two oblique edges vertical edge. gives us different local behaviour depending look. fit random forest ‘caret’ model object can passed ‘lime’ ‘kumquat’.

title: Comparing kumquat with lime
text: lime() builds explainer training data. explain() samples around point, weights samples proximity fits ridge regression. default ‘lime’ bins continuous predictors quartiles, feature weight describes whether point falls particular bin (e.g. y <= -0.49) effect small change value. ask explanation class B, signs comparable ‘kumquat’ .
code: explainer <- lime(train_x, model)  explanation <- explain(   pois[, c("x", "y")],   explainer,   labels = "B",   n_features = 2 )  explanation[, c("case", "feature_desc", "feature_weight", "model_r2")] #> # A tibble: 8 × 4 #>   case  feature_desc            feature_weight model_r2 #>   <chr> <chr>                            <dbl>    <dbl> #> 1 1     x <= -0.4817                    0.232    0.0994 #> 2 1     -0.48171 < y <= 0.00701        -0.250    0.0994 #> 3 2     -0.4817 < x <= 0.0166           0.163    0.0432 #> 4 2     0.00701 < y <= 0.49110          0.159    0.0432 #> 5 3     0.0166 < x <= 0.5060           -0.101    0.0712 #> 6 3     0.49110 < y                     0.272    0.0712 #> 7 4     0.5060 < x                     -0.115    0.0136 #> 8 4     y <= -0.48171                  -0.0476   0.0136 plot_features(explanation, ncol = 2)

title: Comparing kumquat with lime
text: ‘kumquat’ generates regular grid perturbations within radius point, labels model fits L1-penalised logistic regression labels. coefficients original scale predictors describe log-odds second class (B). model bundled, ‘kumquat’ unbundles point interest. lasso drops irrelevant feature horizontal vertical edges, oblique edges ratio two coefficients close slope boundary (0.8). coefficients large , inside small neighbourhood, two classes almost perfectly separated straight line. signs relative sizes matter absolute values. plot_interest() shows perturbations coloured local surrogate’s prediction, point interest black. surrogate good local fit, split colour follows model’s boundary.
code: ks <- kumquat(   model_bundle = bundle::bundle(model),   data = train_x,   pois = pois[, c("x", "y")],   radius = 0.1,   step = 0.01,   predictor_vars = c("x", "y"),   class_names = levels(d_multitwo$class) )  kumquat_imps <- pinch_importance(ks) cbind(pois[, c("poi", "boundary")], kumquat_imps) #>   poi      boundary           x         y #> 1   1    horizontal     0.00000 1001.3399 #> 2   2 upper oblique   -96.98741  135.9254 #> 3   3      vertical -1001.33989    0.0000 #> 4   4 lower oblique   115.34749 -114.3441 wrap_plots(   Map(     \(p, b) p + labs(title = b),     plot_interest(ks),     pois$boundary   ),   ncol = 2,   guides = "collect" )

title: Comparing kumquat with lime
text: methods return signed weight per feature. scales comparable (‘lime’ explains predicted probability ‘kumquat’ explains log-odds), rescale explanation absolute weights sum one. keeps relative importance x y sign one.  example ‘kumquat’ recovers shape piece boundary. ‘lime’ gives weight features every point, signs always agree local boundary, e.g. horizontal edge, moving x change prediction. Things note: Locality. ‘kumquat’ looks inside square side 2 * radius around point, weights reflect boundary passes square. ‘lime’ samples whole training distribution relies kernel focus point. binned features weights mostly describe quartile point falls , can point different direction local boundary. Interpretation weights. ‘kumquat’ coefficient change log-odds B one-unit change predictor near point. ‘lime’ weight change predicted probability B associated point bin. Tuning. ‘kumquat’ set neighbourhood directly radius step, can turn LIME-style kernel weighting weighted = TRUE. ‘lime’ set kernel_width, n_permutations binning options.
code: lime_long <- data.frame(   poi = as.integer(explanation$case),   feature = explanation$feature,   weight = explanation$feature_weight,   method = "lime" )  kumquat_long <- data.frame(   poi = rep(pois$poi, each = 2),   feature = rep(c("x", "y"), times = nrow(pois)),   weight = as.vector(t(as.matrix(kumquat_imps[, c("x", "y")]))),   method = "kumquat" )  compare <- rbind(lime_long, kumquat_long) compare$weight <- ave(   compare$weight,   compare$poi, compare$method,   FUN = \(w) if (all(w == 0)) w else w / sum(abs(w)) ) compare$boundary <- factor(   pois$boundary[compare$poi],   levels = pois$boundary )  ggplot(compare, aes(x = weight, y = feature, fill = method)) +   geom_col(position = "dodge") +   geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +   facet_wrap(~boundary, ncol = 2) +   scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +   labs(x = "Relative weight towards class B", y = NULL) +   theme_minimal()

what: Step 3: Decide on points of interest
title: A Smaller Version of LIME
code: # Decide on points of interest find_closest <- function(pt, data) {   dst <- data |>     mutate(dst = sqrt((x - pt$x)^2 + (y - pt$y)^2))   return(which.min(dst$dst)) }  pois <- c(   # Case 1: the point of interest is not near the boundary   find_closest(tibble(x=0, y=0), d_vertical),   # Case 2: the point is on the decision boundary   find_closest(tibble(x=0.3, y=0.5), d_vertical) ) ggplot(d_vertical, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = class)) +   geom_point() +   geom_point(data=d_vertical[pois, ], mapping=aes(x=x,y=y,fill=class), shape = 18, color = "black") +   scale_colour_discrete_divergingx(palette = "Zissou 1") +   theme_minimal() +   theme(aspect.ratio = 1)

title: kumquat (development version)
text: Added kernel_weights() weight perturbations distance point interest using LIME’s exponential kernel. fit_local_model() now labels surrogate predictions levels pred column factor character vector. Previously labels followed order class_names, passing e.g. unique(data$class) swap . class_names now used numeric (0/1) predictions. fit_local_model() gains weights argument, kumquat() gains weighted, kernel_width dist_fun arguments fit local model proximity weights.
